planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil has warmed past frost risk; this red-skinned, yellow-fleshed variety needs a full season to bulk up its round, shallow-eyed tubers.

directions: Rooster was bred in 1990 at the Teagasc Oak Park research centre in Carlow, Ireland, by potato breeder Harry Kehoe, and went on to dominate Irish potato growing, accounting for roughly a third of national production by the mid-2000s. Plant seed pieces into well-worked, well-drained soil and hill the rows as shoots emerge to keep the dull red skins from greening. The floury yellow flesh holds its shape just enough to make Rooster a true all-rounder in the kitchen, equally good boiled, mashed, roasted, or chipped. Lift maincrop tubers once the foliage dies back in autumn and cure them briefly before storing in a cool, dark, frost-free space.

planting.note: Give this late maincrop variety the longest possible season; its strong blight tolerance makes it forgiving of damp, disease-prone summers.

directions: Cara was released in Ireland in 1973 and remains valued above all for its notably strong resistance to late blight in both foliage and tubers, a trait that let generations of Irish growers skip extra fungicide passes in wet years. The large, round white tubers with faint pink-flushed eyes keep growing late into the season, so leave Cara in the ground longer than early varieties before lifting. Its white flesh is dense and holds together well, making it a favorite for roasting and baking rather than a fluffy mash. Because the thick skin stores exceptionally well, Cara is a dependable choice for a root cellar that needs to carry potatoes deep into winter.

planting.note: A reliable grower on damp ground; its foliage carries above-average late blight resistance, so it can be left standing a little longer in a wet autumn.

directions: Ulster Emblem was bred in 1966 by J. Clarke of Ballymoney, County Antrim, part of a wave of Northern Irish varieties selected specifically for standing up to late blight. The plants carry red-violet flowers and pink sprouts, useful markers for identifying seed stock, before setting long oval tubers with white skin and a semi-waxy white flesh. That semi-waxy texture keeps slices intact through boiling, so it suits potato salads and gratins better than heavy mashing. Harvest once the vines have largely died back, since the variety's main strength is a dependable, disease-resistant yield rather than exceptional earliness.

planting.note: Grows and stores much like its parent Maris Piper; give it a full maincrop season and hill well to keep the developing tubers covered.

directions: Navan was bred in Northern Ireland in 1987 from Maris Piper stock, inheriting that parent's high dry-matter flesh while being selected specifically for frying performance. Plant seed potatoes into loose, fertile soil and hill the rows as growth progresses to prevent the tubers near the surface from greening in the light. Because Navan was bred with chip-shop use in mind, it holds its shape and crisps well when cut into chips or wedges, a step up from boiling-focused varieties. Lift the maincrop once foliage has yellowed and died down, then cure and store tubers in a dark, cool space before use.

planting.note: A rare Irish landrace rather than a modern breeding-program release; grow it as a maincrop and expect smaller yields than commercial cultivars.

directions: Bloomer is an old Irish Midlands landrace first documented in County Clare in 1936 and prized by seed-saving growers for its round tubers with a distinctive purplish-blue skin, deep eyes, and cream-colored flesh. By the mid-1980s it had been identified as a variety found nowhere outside Ireland, which is why heritage seed custodians still keep it in circulation today. Grow it as you would any maincrop potato, hilling the stems as the white-flowered plants grow and leaving the tubers in the ground until the foliage dies back naturally. Because it was never bred for commercial yield, treat Bloomer as a conservation and curiosity crop for the table rather than a high-volume staple, best boiled or roasted in small batches to show off its cream flesh.

planting.note: A long-season heritage variety; give it the full maincrop window and expect tubers closely resembling the famous Irish Lumper in shape.

directions: Irish White was raised around 1882 by Robert Christie of Ballytaggart and became a traditional kitchen-garden potato in County Donegal and County Antrim. The tubers are long and irregularly shaped with white skin and notably deep eyes, closely resembling the famine-era Lumper in form though kept alive today mainly by heritage growers rather than commercial farms. Plant whole or cut seed pieces in deep, loose soil and hill the rows as the plants grow to shade the tubers from sunlight. Give it a full maincrop season before lifting, and expect a historic, old-fashioned potato better suited to boiling and mashing than to modern chip production.

planting.note: A high-yielding variety with good foliar and tuber blight tolerance, making it forgiving in cool, damp maincrop seasons.

directions: Mizen was developed in 1978 at the Teagasc Oak Park breeding centre in County Carlow, part of the same Irish program that later produced Rooster, and was selected for its long, smooth-skinned, creamy yellow tubers and dependable yield. The white flesh carries medium dry matter, giving a texture between waxy and floury that works well for boiling and general cooking. Plant seed pieces in fertile, well-drained soil and hill the rows as shoots emerge, taking advantage of the plant's good resistance to foliar and tuber blight in wetter summers. Lift the crop once the tops die back, since Mizen was bred as a maincrop variety rather than an early one.
